strengths: The paper addresses an important question: how adversarial training can achieve clean generalization and robust training accuracy while retaining poor robust test accuracy. The CGRO definition makes this objective explicit.

The proposed mechanism of learning shared signal while memorizing sample-specific noise is intuitive. Combining representation complexity with feature-learning dynamics is a potentially useful contribution.
Experiments span synthetic data, MNIST, and CIFAR10. The additional input-gradient and local-flatness measurements provide useful qualitative observations beyond classification accuracy.
weaknesses: Theorem 4.4 is false under its stated assumptions. Consider equal probability on ±e_1, radius δ=1/4, and f_clean(x)=x_1−7/8. Assumptions 4.1–4.3 hold, including perfect clean accuracy and nonzero robust error. With sufficiently many samples, both atoms have empirical frequencies near 1/2, so vanishing robust training error forces zero robust test error. CGRO is therefore impossible. Additional assumptions controlling the distribution and sample coverage are essential.

The representation proof contains further substantive errors. Assumption 4.2 separates opposite classes; it does not imply that all training perturbation balls are disjoint, as Lemma 4.5's argument assumes. Appendix F also claims uniform o(1) approximation of a generally discontinuous indicator-based classifier by continuous ReLU networks. Smoothing requires transition-region and classification-margin control that is not supplied.

Theorem 5.9 uses inconsistent threat models. Training in Definitions 5.4–5.6 permits perturbations only along the meaningful signal in one patch, leaving memorized noise unchanged. CGRO in Definitions 3.2–3.4 uses the entire perturbation ball. Small loss against the restricted adversary does not establish the claimed vanishing robust training error against the full adversary. This undermines a central part of the dynamics result.

The population-error proof in Appendix E.12 is not sound. Cubic Gaussian projections are not sub-Gaussian, contrary to the concentration argument used for clean generalization. The proof also infers that every residual weight has norm Θ(1) from aggregate noise-memorization quantities without justification. These steps support the principal test-error guarantees and require substantial repair.

The synthetic experiment does not satisfy the theorem's crucial radius assumption: Section 6.2 sets δ=α=10, whereas Assumption 5.7 requires δ<α. The attack can then erase the meaningful signal completely. Poor robust test performance in this setting cannot distinguish the proposed learning mechanism from information loss caused by the attack, and does not validate the stated theorem.

The auxiliary global-flatness bound in Theorem B.1 is also false as stated. A classifier with constant nonzero output has zero input gradients, but its logistic loss varies by label. Sampling fluctuations in class proportions can therefore make empirical loss smaller than population loss with probability approaching 1/2, even with smooth class-conditional densities. The claimed bound incorrectly eliminates this deviation whenever global flatness is zero.

The claimed advance over Li et al. (2022) needs clarification. Theorem 4.7 is existential over distributions, and Appendix F still constructs a linearly separable hard instance. Replacing linear separability with existence of a polynomial-size clean classifier does not itself establish a stronger lower bound. Furthermore, an existential worst-case bound does not explain the capacity requirements of the practical datasets studied.

The empirical evaluation does not isolate representation limitations from optimization failure: small MNIST models collapsing to chance accuracy is insufficient evidence of inadequate expressive capacity. PGD iteration counts, step sizes, restarts, key optimization settings, and variability across runs are insufficiently documented. These omissions limit reproduction and confidence in the reported robustness measurements.
